newsitem.title: USA: Clinton adviser sees full agenda on global economy.
newsitem.headline: Clinton adviser sees full agenda on global economy.

text.p: Daniel Tarullo, named by President Clinton as a top policy adviser on the international economy, said Friday he looked forward to a full agenda in helping to advance U.S. interests abroad.

"We have a lot to do in the next couple of years, not only with our ongoing agenda but with our hosting of the (Group of Seven) economic summit next June in Denver," Tarullo said after Clinton named him to the newly created post of Assistant to the President for International Economic Policy.
International economic issues are gaining in importance, Tarullo said, while praising the president for recognizing their importance by establishing the new position.
"At the beginning of this century, America was evolving from a regional to a national economy," Tarullo said. "As we enter the next century we are becoming part of an evolving global economy."

Among the more immediate international economic issues that may occupy some of Tarullo's time include concerns about the potential impact on U.S. stock and bond markets should foreign investors halt their buying or decide to sell.

Some analysts have said that Japanese investors, in particular, may slow their purchases of U.S. Treasuries because of concerns that the dollar's climb against the yen may be coming to an end for the time being.

Tarullo, a 44-year-old former Harvard Law School professor, has labored for nearly two years in the shadows as the White House "sherpa" who prepares for the Group of Seven (G7) economic summits. Tarullo has worked in a series of jobs at the State, Justice and Commerce Departments as well as on Capitol Hill, where he served as chief counsel to Sen. Edward Kennedy, the influential Massachusetts Democrat.
But his most delicate government assignment has come during the past 21 months, when he has been Clinton's personal representative to the Group of Seven industrialized nations.
The position, known in government circles as the "sherpa" because it prepares the path to G7 summits, involves the most delicate matters of international economic policy, such as exchange rates.

In the job, Tarullo was responsible for sitting down with his counterparts from the other G7 members -- Britain, France, Germany, Italy, Canada and Japan -- to hammer out positions on issues that are often contentious, to say the least.

Tarullo joined the Clinton administration in July 1993 as the assistant secretary of state for economic and business affairs and in March 1995 was given the added responsibility of the G7 assignment. In March 1996, he moved to the White House as deputy assistant to the president for economic policy.
Before that he worked at the Shearman and Sterling law firm, concentrating on antitrust, securities and international transactions.

Tarullo worked in the Justice Department's antitrust division in 1978 and 1979 and at the Commerce Department in 1980 and 1981, when he left to teach at the Harvard Law School. He stayed there until 1987.
He served as Kennedy's chief counsel from 1987 to 1989.
A native of Boston, Tarullo received his bachelor's degree from Georgetown University in 1973 and a law degree from the University of Michigan in 1977.
